summary: Describes Microsoft Point-to-Point Encryption, which protects the confidentiality of PPP-encapsulated packets. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This puts a lock on the messages sent over a dial-up style connection so outsiders cannot read them.

questions: how does mppe protect ppp connections
what encryption strengths does mppe support
what happens if packets are lost in mppe
subtitle: Encrypts Point-to-Point Protocol packets using the RC4 algorithm.

tldr.problem: PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) connections, typically used for dial-up Internet access, transmit data in the clear, exposing user traffic to eavesdropping.
tldr.mechanism: MPPE (Microsoft Point-To-Point Encryption) adds encryption to PPP using the RC4 stream cipher. It negotiates encryption strength (40-bit, 56-bit, or 128-bit keys), maintains a 12-bit coherency counter to keep encryption tables synchronized, and can change keys frequently—either after every packet (stateless mode) or at regular intervals (stateful mode).
tldr.outcome: PPP links can negotiate encryption transparently, protecting confidentiality end-to-end. The scheme does not require reliable transmission and does not add data expansion. However, it has known weaknesses in stateful mode when packets are lost.

facts.label: Key change frequency
facts.value: Stateless: every packet; Stateful: every 256 packets

today: RFC 3078 is informational and updates RFC 2118. MPPE was widely used for securing PPP dial-up connections in the 1990s and 2000s. Today, with the decline of PPP dial-up access and the prevalence of VPNs and TLS, MPPE is largely obsolete. The RC4 cipher, while used here, has known cryptographic weaknesses and is deprecated in many modern protocols.

sections.title: What MPPE Does
sections.content:
Microsoft Point-To-Point Encryption (MPPE) protects the confidentiality of data transmitted over PPP connections. PPP is the protocol used for dial-up and some broadband Internet access; MPPE encrypts the packets that flow through a PPP link using the RSA RC4 stream cipher.

MPPE negotiates the strength of encryption (40-bit, 56-bit, or 128-bit keys) and the encryption mode (stateless or stateful) during connection setup. Once negotiated, all eligible packets are encrypted transparently using the agreed parameters. The protocol does not compress data, does not require reliable delivery, and does not expand the packet size.
sections.eli5: MPPE scrambles your dial-up or PPP connection so no one listening on the line can read your data.

sections.title: Negotiation and Configuration
sections.content:
MPPE is negotiated as an option (type 18) in the CCP (Compression Control Protocol), which is part of PPP. During negotiation, each peer advertises the encryption strengths it supports using bit flags: the L bit for 40-bit keys, the M bit for 56-bit keys, and the S bit for 128-bit keys. The H bit indicates support for stateless mode, where the session key changes after every packet.

The responder SHOULD select the strongest encryption option offered by the initiator. If negotiation fails and one party attempted MPPE, the connection SHOULD be terminated rather than falling back to unencrypted communication. This prevents accidental transmission of unencrypted data when encryption was requested.
sections.eli5: Before the connection starts, the two computers decide how strong the scrambling should be and whether to change the scrambling key often.

sections.title: Packet Structure and Encryption
sections.content:
MPPE packets are sent with PPP protocol type 0x00FD when encrypted. Each packet has a 4-byte header containing the original PPP protocol field (which is also encrypted), a 4-bit flags field, and a 12-bit coherency count. The coherency count is a monotonically increasing counter that wraps at 4,095, allowing the receiver to detect missing packets.

Only packets with protocol numbers in the range 0x0021 to 0x00FA are encrypted (like IP packets); other control packets pass through unencrypted. The D bit in the header indicates whether the packet is actually encrypted. The A bit (FLUSHED) signals that the encryption tables have been reinitialized and MUST be set on every packet in stateless mode.
sections.eli5: Each encrypted packet has a counter so both sides know which packets are missing, and a flag that says whether the key was just reset.

sections.title: Key Management and Session Keys
sections.content:
MPPE uses session keys derived from peer credentials (such as authentication tokens from CHAP or MS-CHAP). Once a session key is established, the RC4 cipher is initialized with it. Data is then encrypted by passing it through the RC4 stream cipher.

Keys can be changed frequently. In stateless mode, the session key changes after every packet—the sender changes its key before encrypting each packet, and the receiver changes its key after receiving each packet. In stateful mode, keys change less frequently: when the low byte of the coherency count reaches 0xFF (the "flag" packet). If stateless mode is negotiated, the FLUSHED bit MUST be set on every packet so the receiver can resynchronize.
sections.eli5: Both sides use a secret number (the session key) to initialize the scrambler. They can change the secret number often, either after every message or every 256 messages.

sections.title: Synchronization and Packet Loss
sections.content:
MPPE uses the coherency count to keep encryption tables synchronized when packets are lost. In stateless mode, if the received coherency count is higher than expected, the receiver performs multiple key changes to catch up. The FLUSHED bit ensures resynchronization, so no CCP Reset-Request packets are needed.

In stateful mode, synchronization is trickier. If a "flag" packet (coherency count ending in 0xFF) is lost, the receiver will not know to change its key. If the coherency count then wraps around, the receiver detects the out-of-order count, sends a CCP Reset-Request, and waits for a packet with the FLUSHED bit set before resuming decryption. For this reason, stateful mode SHOULD NOT be used on lossy networks (like the Internet) where packets are frequently dropped.
sections.eli5: If messages get lost, the computers use a counter to notice and fix themselves. Stateful mode is risky on slow networks where messages often disappear.

fields.name: PPP Protocol
fields.desc: The original PPP protocol field (also encrypted).

fields.name: Flags (A, B, C, D)
fields.desc: A = FLUSHED (tables reinitialized), D = encrypted flag.

fields.name: Coherency Count
fields.desc: Packet sequence number (0 to 4095, wraps to 0).
